speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was with deep regret that we learned just a few hours ago that another member of this house had quite unexpectedly passed away. I refer to Mr. Charles Delmar Coyle, the hon. member for Elgin, who was with us last week and whom I think most of us regarded as enjoying good health.
Mr. Coyle was born in Kinglake, Ontario, in 1887, and educated there. He was a farmer and tobacco grower, and he also found time to render outstanding service to his fellow citizens in his community. This service included that of occupying the positions of reeve of Bayham township and warden of Elgin county.
He was first elected to the House of Commons for the constituency of Elgin in 1945, and successfully contested that seat in both elections since that date.
He took a keen interest in the work of parliament and made a real contribution to the work of the committees of which he was a member. In fact, I understand he expected as recently as yesterday to be with us today, and to attend meetings with officials of the government. He always worked hard and conscientiously to serve the best possible interests of his constituency and of the country. That his efforts were appreciated is well indicated by the fact that he was returned at the last election with a substantial majority. During his lifetime he established a fine reputation for his industry and publicspiritedness and for his personal integrity.
I should like to extend to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) and to members of his party our sincere sympathy in the loss of a valuable member; and to Mrs. Coyle and her family our very sincere condolences in her and their bereavement.

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of ihe Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know that all members of the Conservative party will appreciate very much the expression of sympathy extended by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent); and that Mrs. Coyle and her two sons and her daughter will greatly appreciate
the sympathy expressed by the Prime Minister on behalf of all the members of the House of Commons.
It does come as a great shock to all of us who were closely associated with him, as I know it does to every member, to see a man suddenly leave us in this way when he was in apparently the very best of health, even until last night. He was here in the house last Friday until the house adjourned at ten o'clock. There are members here who walked down with him from the house on that occasion just prior to his departure for home where he stayed over last night to attend a meeting of a service club in his own riding in order to be associated, as he has been for so many years, with those who have served that community.
Like many others in this house, as the Prime Minister has already mentioned, Charlie Coyle, as we all knew him and shall continue to know him, had served his own community in many capacities and for many years. He had that ground work of public service that comes through association with municipal council. He was a councillor for years, then he was reeve of his own township, and then he received the highest honour that can be conferred in the local municipalities in the rural areas when he became warden of his own county. He was highly respected and greatly loved by all who knew him.
One of the things that make it so difficult to realize even yet that he has left us is that with his lovable and friendly qualities he had made a wide circle of friends, which I know embraced every member of this house.
I do hope there will be some very real measure of comfort for his family in their tragic and sudden loss in the knowledge that his associates are thinking of his family at this time and sharing, at least in some measure, their sorrow in the loss of a devoted public servant.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to associate myself and all members of the C.C.F. group in the expressions of sympathy and appreciation that have been made by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) in regard to the death of Mr. Coyle.
During the last parliament Mr. Coyle sat over here on this side very close to us.

The late C. D. Coyle
Generally speaking, I have found that when you get fairly close to people and get more or less to know their intimate thoughts, you find that there is a great deal of humour and, if I may say so, a great many lovable qualities about them. That is how we felt about Mr. Coyle. When we see members from back here, we just glare at one another; but when we get as close to members as we are to our friends here, we find that they are really a good bunch of fellows; and Mr. Coyle was one of the best.
We wish to extend our sympathy to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) and his party, and to Mr. Coyle's relatives.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to associate this group for which I speak with the tributes which have been paid to the late hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Coyle) and to extend to his family and to his party in the house our sincere sympathy in the loss of a very fine man and follower.

Mr. Speaker, it is on an occasion such as this that we probably get to appreciate one another better when we lay aside for a moment or two the cares of the country and of parliament and consider our friend who has passed on. It has been my privilege to know him through three parliaments. He has been my roommate for some five years. I came to know Mr. Coyle very intimately; and I agree with the words of other members who have spoken previously. I know that he was a man of integrity. He was a man of good judgment. I greatly respected his opinion on the various matters that came up from day to day. I can only join with those who have already spoken in paying my tribute to him and in conveying my condolences and sorrow to the bereaved family.

speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. speechtext:
My hon. friend was kind enough to give me notice of his question. He asks first of all what, pursuant to the inquiry made of my officers in my absence, was the situation resulting from communications made by the Department of National Health and Welfare to the appropriate departments of health of the provinces of

Saskatchewan and Alberta. Contact has been made with the officers in the two departments of the two provinces. The facts of the matter have been ascertained. The responsibility for remedying the situation is recognized by both provinces as not coming within the competence of the federal government. speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 77, to amend the acts respecting the Northwest Territories.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the bill to amend the acts respecting the Northwest Territories is divided into two parts. As I explained at the resolution stage, it is necessary to amend both the existing Northwest Territories Act and the new Northwest Territories Act which will not be proclaimed until after the new Criminal Code is enacted. The amendments to the existing act are contained in part I of the bill, and the amendments to the new act are contained in part II.
When we were at the resolution stage, Mr. Speaker, I explained some of the purposes of the bill as they are mentioned in the explanatory notes in the bill. The purposes which I have already discussed are as follows:
(a) to provide that the governor in council may, after the expiration of two years from the return of the writs of election of elected members of the council, dissolve the council and cause a new council to be elected and appointed;
(c)	to add provisions relating to reindeer and penalties similar to those already included in chapter 331;
(e) to provide that the governor in council may appoint a member of the council in place of an elected member who resigns.
Other amendments will increase the time within which copies of ordinances enacted by the territorial council are to be transmitted to the governor in council from 10 days to 30 days, and raise the living allowance payable to members of council from $15 to $25 per day. Both these provisions are already contained in the new Northwest Territories Act, chapter 331 of the Revised Statutes of 1952.
Both the existing act and the new act are to be amended to clarify the provision relating to indemnity and living allowances, and to include provisions relating to the holding of land similar to those added to the Yukon Act by chapter 53 of the Statutes of 1952-53. This amendment is necessary in order that

the territorial government may hold title to public buildings constructed with territorial funds.
Another amendment to both acts provides for authority being given to the territorial government to enter into agreements with the government of Canada under and for the purposes of any act which authorizes the federal government to enter into agreements with the provinces. This will enable the territorial government to receive assistance under any such acts in the same manner as the provinces are now receiving it. As an example, I might mention that negotiations are now under way for assistance being given under the Vocational Training Coordination Act, which will be made possible when the bill is passed.
In the course of the debate on December 10 on the resolution for introduction of the present bill, the Leader of the Opposition suggested that it would be desirable to take advantage of this amendment to increase the elected representation on the council of the Northwest Territories. The council legislates for the territories, in the manner of a provincial legislature, and also advises the commissioner on questions referred to it. At the present time the council consists of 8 members, of whom 3 are elected and 5 are appointed by the governor in council. The Leader of the Opposition proposed that the number of elected representatives should be raised so that "they will balance the appointed representatives and give greater opportunity for representation, consistent with the same contact with the government."
Following the hon. member's suggestion I undertook to discuss the matter with the members of the Northwest Territories council who were meeting in Ottawa at that time.
The question of the size of the council and of its composition is, of course, not one that comes within the jurisdiction of the council itself. However, the matter was discussed informally with its members. I may say to the Leader of the Opposition that the general feeling of the members, both elected and appointed, was that there is a great deal of merit in his suggestion. They were unanimously of the opinion that, if the government were disposed to recommend such a change, they would be in favour of an amendment to the Northwest Territories Act that would provide for some increase in elected representation.
With regard to the extent of any increase in representation that might be made at this time, the feeling of the members was that account had to be taken of the varying degree of development of the different parts of the Northwest Territories. At the present time
Northwest Territories
much the largest proportion of the population of the territories is concentrated in the western part of the district of Mackenzie- particularly in the basin of the Mackenzie river itself. The 3 constituencies that send elected members to the council are all in the district of Mackenzie. There are no elected representatives from any part of the districts of Keewatin or Franklin, which make up the eastern part of the mainland and the Arctic islands. The view of the members of the council was that the population and state of development of the districts of Keewatin and Franklin is not such at the present time that it would be desirable, or even feasible, to have an elected member from a constituency that covered those areas, or any part of them. They consider, however, that the objective should be to have a member from that part of the territories as soon as the development and the growth of population justifies it.
In the circumstances, the members of the council were of the opinion that the best course at this time would be to amend the Northwest Territories Act to increase the elected representation from three to four. The fourth constituency would be inserted in the district of Mackenzie. The definition of the boundaries of the constituencies is done by ordinance of the council of the Northwest Territories. It is not a matter for this parliament.
The necessary changes would be made before the next election in the territories, which will probably take place in September, 1954. Provision for the fifth elected member, which the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) had in mind, would be held in reserve for a further amendment at a later date when the growth and development of the territories has made it clear that the addition is desirable and has shown more clearly just what the area should be that the additional representative would cover.
That is the advice of the members of the council of the Northwest Territories. Since they themselves feel that the fifth elected position ought to be held in reserve, I think that is the best course to follow. Up until 1951 there was no elected representation on the council at all. The proposed increase of one will be an indication of the kind and direction of the progress in self-government that is desirable. Further development will come as circumstances justify it.
In view of the importance of this proposal to the people of the Northwest Territories, I have discussed it with my colleagues and I am glad to advise the Leader of the Opposition that, at the appropriate stage in the

Northwest Territories
consideration of the present bill, I shall ask one of my colleagues to move an additional amendment which will increase the size of the council of the Northwest Territories from eight members to nine, and the number of elected members from three to four.

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of ihe Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ELECTIONS, APPOINTMENTS TO COUNCIL, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the statement by the minister that the government has decided to make this increase from three to four, and welcome, too, the manner in which the statement has been made. It is encouraging to feel that, out of a discussion of this kind, we can find a substantial measure of agreement in matters of great importance for the years ahead.
I accept without any criticism or objection the suggestion by the minister that the decision to designate a fifth area in which there would be an elected member for the time being should stand in abeyance. I would have welcomed a decision to do this at the present time; but I think there is a great deal of merit in the view he has expressed.
The important thing is that a decision to increase the number of elected representatives is positive evidence to the people in northern Canada, as well as the people in other parts of this country whose interest we wish to arouse in the north, that there is a steady movement toward elected representation for that area.
By the standards of representation in the southern areas of Canada, the numbers in those northern parts are small. It is not likely that at any time there will be a great concentration of population in the north. Nevertheless within a comparatively few years we have seen enormous changes taking place. It is only a few years ago that there was practically no mineral area of importance in the north, with the exception of the romantic Yukon. Since then we have seen the discovery of increasing quantities of rich ore of different kinds. The Northwest Territories have played a vitally important part in the development of atomic energy. In many ways the north beckons to the young and the vigorous, to people of all ages, who look for the rewards that come with adventure and with new developments such as we have seen in that part of Canada.
I appreciate the words in which the minister announced the decision of the government. I should hope the fact that we can find such a substantial measure of agreement as to the desirability of dramatizing in some measure the move toward greater representation in the northern area would be a happy augury of the approach to be made to the broad problems of that great internal empire. Numbers
[Mr. Lesage.I
of population are small. I agree with the minister that in the Keewatin and Franklin areas it would be so small that it would be difficult to have separate representation there at the moment, with any sense of reality. Nevertheless we recall that the Franklin area is one of the historic sections of Canada. Who can tell that any part of that great northland will not provide new opportunities in the years ahead.
All Canadians should regard the north as an important area for development. There are reasons why the government and parliament should seek in every way to encourage increased population in that area.
We speak often about our neighbours to the south, but not nearly so often in friendly terms about our neighbours to the west and north. Yet, the fact is that only a little more than 50 miles of open water separates this continent from the mainland of Russia. Our great northland is of vital importance in many ways. I do not often speak of Russia as offering us examples of desirable things, but I must say it is worth noting that Russia has been devoting a great deal of attention to the development of its northland, and to the opening of new possibilities for supporting population in that area. We will hope that those developments will be for peace rather than for war-peace that will provide opportunities for us and for other people.
I would hope that in every way possible we would direct our attention to that distant area so as to encourage young Canadians and others who have not yet come to Canada to seek opportunity there. I welcome the minister's statement today respecting the proposed change and accept it as a gesture on the part of the government which will be welcomed by parliament, and as an indication that we are interested in the expansion and development of the north.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ELECTIONS, APPOINTMENTS TO COUNCIL, ETC.
speechtext:
A few moments ago the minister said that in 1951 the Northwest Territories Act provided for the first elected representatives to sit on that council. Prior to that time, in 1946, I think it was, the act provided for the appointment of a resident of the territory to sit on the council. In the case in question, if a member dies or resigns, provision should be made for a by-election to permit the people to tell us whom they want to send down here. It has been said, and I agree, that in the Northwest Territories it is very difficult to hold an election at certain times of the year. For the first eighteen months after an election of those members, a by-election should be held to fill a vacancy. It would be the only democratic thing for us to do to replace, by means of a by-election within the first eighteen months after the election, a member who dies or resigns. In the case of an appointment after eighteen months the act should provide-and I hope the minister will agree-for the appointment of a resident of the constituency that was represented by the man who died or resigned.
I feel strongly on this. If we are going to act in a democratic way we should make the appointment from residents of the constituency of the man who died or resigned. That is all I have to say.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ELECTIONS, APPOINTMENTS TO COUNCIL, ETC.
speechtext:
There is a great deal in the
representations and suggestions which have just been made by the hon. member for Mackenzie River and we have considered the suggestions.
May I point out first of all that in 1946 the act did not provide-as a matter of fact no act ever provided-for the appointment of a resident of the territory. That was a matter of policy which was followed in the appointments, but the act never provided for it.
The hon. member himself has mentioned one of the difficulties of having by-elections in the north. We can have effective byelections or elections in the north in a period of only three or four months, at the most, in the year. We feel that every constituency should be represented as far as possible at every session of the council. At the last session of the council, following the resignation of the then member of the council who has since taken his seat here, the constituency could not be represented because the act did not provide for the replacement of a member who resigned; it provided only for the replacement of a member who died. Provision for the replacement of a member who died was by appointment because of the very high cost of holding elections in the territories.

Northwest Territories
Second, the government wanted to be sure that every constituency would be represented at meetings of the council. It would not have been possible to hold a by-election in the Northwest Territories following the resignation of the then member, Mr. Hardie, who is now the hon. member for Mackenzie River in this house, before the meeting of the session of the council last December.
May I give a few figures on the cost of elections in the Northwest Territories. I might mention that appropriation for expenditures of $1,236.73 was made in connection with the plenary conference held between representatives of the chief electoral office and the three returning officers. This was the only item of expenditure made by this administration in connection with these territorial elections. The other expenditures were made by the chief electoral officer out of his own funds. I have obtained from him details of expenditure broken down by electoral districts and these are as follows: Mackenzie West-a little over $7,000; Mackenzie South-$2,677; Mackenzie North- $3,664.96. That is a total of over $13,000, and that is apart from the appropriation made by the territorial council itself under [DOT]ordinance No. 1, dated February 15, 1951, providing for the sum of $11,000 for the cost of elections.
As to the suggested inclusion in the act of a condition that an appointment be conferred only upon a resident of a constituency, it seems to me that is more a matter of policy than one of legislation. No member of this house has to reside in his constituency in order to be elected. I feel that is a matter for the electors themselves to decide. I believe we should not create a precedent by requiring the appointed representative to reside in the district. On the other hand, I wish to assure hon. members that, unless there is something very exceptional, this government will see to it that any appointment that has to be made in accordance with that section of the act will be conferred upon a resident of the constituency wherein the vacancy occurs.

[Mr. Lesage.l

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ELECTIONS, APPOINTMENTS TO COUNCIL, ETC.
speechtext:
It is true, Mr. Chairman, that when we were at the resolution stage I undertook to give the hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra some information regarding musk-ox. I have some here which I will give now if he wishes to have it.
In the early days of the fur trade a great number of musk-ox robes were taken. This led to a great reduction in numbers on the Canadian mainland. Exploration and development in the high Arctic led to similar reductions on many of the islands. The animals are easily destroyed as they form a defensive circle when attacked. This repels the wolves but leaves the musk-ox vulnerable to the rifle.
In 1917 the musk-oxen were given total protection and the export of robes from Canada prohibited. In 1927 the Thelon game sanctuary was established to protect the last stronghold of the species on the mainland, which area was thought to contain 250 animals. By 1937 the population was estimated at 290, and under continued protection the sanctuary population has continued to grow to the present estimate of 600 to 1,000.
In 1930 the total Canadian musk-ox population was estimated to be about 14,000 animals, 500 of which occurred on the mainland. In 1937 the mainland estimate rose to 1,200. The mainland population has continued to grow, though improved transportation facilities have no doubt led to increased musk-ox sightings and consequent apparent increases in population figures. At present herds outside of the Thelon game sanctuary are known to occur at the following localities: north of Great Bear lake, 90 animals; Bathurst inlet, 500 animals; and in the vicinity of Pelly bay where there is no count.

124&
The recent increased aerial reconnaissance in the Canadian Arctic archipelago has added considerable information to our knowledge of musk-ox distribution in that area. They are known to occur on Banks, Victoria, Prince Patrick, Melville, Eglinton, Bathurst, Cornwallis, Devon, Graham, Axel Heiberg and Ellesmere islands. The population on Ellesmere island is considerable. Herds of 500 and 200 have been estimated on the Fosheim peninsula and south coast respectively. There is every reason to believe that the population of this interesting Arctic mammal will continue to increase under proper management and may yet yield valuable products for the Arctic economy.
May I also mention at this point that when we were at the resolution stage some very high figures were mentioned for the population of reindeer. Following that discussion there has been mention in one newspaper, I believe, of the population of reindeer in Alaska as being 20 million. A few zeros should have been taken from that figure, for it is 20,000.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ELECTIONS, APPOINTMENTS TO COUNCIL, ETC.
speechtext:
Are there economic possibilities for the musk-ox herds in the north? My question of course is based on the article in Maclean's magazine for August, 1951, by Vilhjalmur Stefansson. In that article he referred particularly to the musk-ox. He seemed to place more importance on them than on reindeer. He told of spending a year on uninhabited Melville island which is north of the 75th parallel. He went to to say:
Our chief source of food was the shaggy, sheeplike, hulking ovibos, often miscalled musk-ox . . . The meat is excellent, the hair makes a wool finer than cashmere and does not shrink when dyed or washed.
He went on to say that a magnificent way to use much of the otherwise forbidding northern land would be by using it for the development of musk-ox herds. He then said:
The musk-ox, whose feeding habits are even better suited to the north than the reindeer, could do far better. I estimate that Canada's north could maintain a hundred million musk-ox, which is the equivalent of 400 million sheep. What such a vast industry would do for Canada, and what such supplies of food might do to assist in other developments of the north such as mining and oil, I leave to your imagination.
Those figures may be much too high but even if they are within shooting distance of the truth this development might be very significant. Can the minister tell us whether or not Stefansson was reasonably accurate in his statement?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ELECTIONS, APPOINTMENTS TO COUNCIL, ETC.
speechtext:
The information given by Stefansson is of course accurate. The musk-ox can be used for its fur and for its meat, but it is because there are so few musk-ox that 83276-79J
Northwest Territories
we have to prohibit their killing. One thing must not be forgotten. While the annual increase of reindeer is about 25 per cent the annual increase of musk-ox is not more than 10 per cent. Musk-ox females have their calves only every two years. The rate of increase is very slow. We have to protect them, and it is still too early to think of drawing any economic benefits from the musk-ox which, by the way, is a wild animal while the reindeer is domestic.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ELECTIONS, APPOINTMENTS TO COUNCIL, ETC.
speechtext: I hope it is the policy of the department to build up herds of both these animals. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ELECTIONS, APPOINTMENTS TO COUNCIL, ETC.
speechtext: That is correct. That is our policy, and that is why we have very strict regulations, in order that we may increase the population of both reindeer and musk-ox to the extent where they will be an economic, asset in the development of the north.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ELECTIONS, APPOINTMENTS TO COUNCIL, ETC.
speechtext:
I do not know whether the minister will remember that the last time this: subject was under discussion I brought to his attention certain allegations-they appeared to me to be allegations-that had been made in a book which I think should deeply touch our consciences, namely, "People of the Deer" by Farley Mowat. I am not sure, but I think that at that time the minister said he would look into the subject and see what he could tell me about it when this measure came up in committee. If the allegations contained in the book are true, it is a terrible indictment of neglect upon the part of somebody, and I do not know anybody better to blame than the department of the dominion government that handles these affairs.
It is true that some of Mr. Mowat's assertions were denied publicly, and to that denial he replied in terms which I see no reason to disbelieve. His allegations were that a certain tribe of Eskimos, who are not sea-going Eskimos and are not even found along the seacoast, have been allowed through various circumstances to disintegrate, and that in fact their numbers were decreased and even depleted by starvation. The theme of the book is that the natural way these people live is through the use of their natural food, the reindeer. They were coaxed away from their natural manner of life, and I think in some cases there is an allegation made against the Hudson's Bay Company. I did note that the Hudson's Bay Company was severely critical of the book, and I believe approached the library authorities of the provincial government in Toronto suggesting that perhaps the book should be removed from the shelves. I do not know whether or not that is true,, but that is what I have heard.

Northwest Territories
Now, the allegation is that these people were separated from their ordinary means of livelihood; that they were induced to work for private companies, notably certain fishing companies, and when the market for fish disappeared, these people were thrown back on their natural resources, but at that time the natural resources, the caribou, were not available. I have been able to give only an incomplete resume of the whole situation, but I should like to know if the minister has anything to tell us about it. It is a rather serious business. It involves the lives of people. It involves their extermination by starvation. As a matter of fact, the regulations concerning the preservation of caribou have improved, and I am glad to see that this section provides for that.
I was interested enough to write to my friend the minister of natural resources in Saskatchewan, Mr. Brockelbank. I need not read the whole of the letter. I was protesting that the government allowed hunting parties to go up there, particularly in aeroplanes, to bag these caribou. I am glad to say he has informed me the practice has been stopped, and that the year 1950-51 was the last year in which caribou were killed for sport. I take it these regulations in the bill will be strictly enforced. Mr. Brockelbank suggested that perhaps the worst offenders were not these outside people who came to enjoy the sport. By the way, I imagine it is an expensive sport and that most of the hunters come from south of the line in their own aeroplanes. It was suggested that the Eskimo themselves were not guiltless in the matter. I quote from his letter where he says:
However, I would point out that much more important in the question of preservation of the caribou is the conservation of the herds by the native people themselves. Too often in the past they have wantonly slaughtered the caribou for dog feed . . .
He goes on with some other matters that are not relative to the question. The thought of people dying out there for want of assistance certainly touched my conscience, if it did not touch the conscience of the people in the department.
I made some inquiries of the department in the last parliament by putting questions on the order paper. I have to say that the replies I received were not adequate. I would not like to call them evasive, but they certainly were not satisfactory to me at that time. I am informed now that this tribe, the so-called Ihalmiut-I am not suggesting that people should copy my pronunciation because I do not know how it should be pronounced- are now subsisting largely on the charity of the members of some military expedition

in that north country. The assertions are that such aid as the government did send to them, when it finally was seized of the importance of the question, was too little and too late. For example, white flour is not much good to an Eskimo.
I have covered a lot of ground. I have to admit my ignorance of the subject, but one of the purposes of a discussion in committee of the whole is to find out these things. Some time ago I gave the minister a warning that I would pursue the question. I notice he shakes his head, which means he has no recollection of such a warning. It was the former minister. In any event, I should like to have his comments on this matter.

Porsild. While I do not wish to go into the whole matter, I may say that I have read Mr. Mowat's reply.

It is a matter which should be cleared up, in the public interest. Of course what is bygone is bygone; we cannot bring back lives. I bring this to the attention of the House of Commons, the department and the public generally in the hope that things like this will not occur again and that we may have more prompt action on behalf of people who are in difficult circumstances and people for whom, as in this instance, we have assumed responsibility.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext:
During the discussion of the last order of business a remark was made about a certain developmental period in relation to that piece of legislation. Bill No. 7 has had an even longer period of development. A royal commission was set up to inquire into it, on February 3, 1949.
That commission reported in January, 1952, and the first bill consolidating the Criminal Code was introduced in the other place in May, 1952. At the end of that session it died on the order paper in the other place. It was then redrafted in the light of discussions in the other place and its committee and reintroduced in the other place in the fall session of 1952. It was reported from the other place on December 16 of that year with no less than 116 amendments.
That bill then came to the House of Commons in the early part of 1953 and was sent to a special committee of this house where it received detailed consideration, section by section, from beginning to end; and it was reported, as those members of the present house who were in the last parliament will recall, with some 70-odd amendments in addition to those which had been made by the other place.
The bill therefore which we are about to consider in committee has already received a very great deal of consideration indeed; first by the royal commission for a period of some three years, then by the drafting officers of the Department of Justice, then by the other place in two separate legislative sessions and by its committees, and finally at the last session of parliament by a special committee of the House of Commons.
Hence it should not be surprising if it would be possible for us in considering the sections of the bill in committee of the whole perhaps to be able to approve of them in an expeditious manner. To that end 1 would suggest there is no better method than to follow the procedure that was followed with great success in the committees of the other place and in the special committee of the House of Commons, namely that the sections should be called one by one.
Our experience in these other committees was that the great majority of sections, being merely a re-enactment of sections of the present Criminal Code which have been the law for a long period of time, are passed without comment. When we came to some particular section or group of sections of a more serious character, such as, for example, those relating to sedition, treason, criminal liability and the like, if any of the opposition

parties or for that matter the government members wish to examine such sections more carefully, we set them aside for this purpose. In the same way now, with a view perhaps to reconsidering the conclusion in relation to such clause which has been recommended by the special committee of the House of Commons, we might set aside such sections and come back and consider them after we had gone through the whole bill. In that way we can proceed with some expedition through the whole bill, and then come back and give regard to the difficult sections separately at the end.
I am sure I do not need to emphasize that the Criminal Code as we have it deals with a large group of subject matters that in the United Kingdom, which does not possess a criminal code, are covered by some 150-odd separate statutes. Each of these subject matters to which I have referred, such for example as treason and sedition, is most important. If therefore we feel that we should not accept the conclusions to which the committees of the other place and the special committee of the House of Commons have come, then I think we owe it to ourselves and the people who sent us here to give very serious consideration and subject to carefully considered debate every matter that is reserved in that way.
With that in view I would suggest that we might start consideration of the bill section by section. If there is any question in relation to any one of them which can be disposed of by brief discussion, then we might deal with those now and pass it. If we come to any question that promises to develop into a more serious debate, perhaps it would be better to set it aside and come back to it later on.

This is a continuation of the idea that was considered in part by the preceding section, concerning which the hon. member asked some questions. This is the section which states that from now on all of the offences for which a Canadian can be tried must be those which are covered by this bill. From now on it will not be possible, in Canada, to charge a Canadian with a common law offence. If the crime for which he is to be charged cannot be found within the limits of the Canadian Criminal Code or another act of parliament, then he cannot be charged at all.
It might be thought, perhaps, that in adopting the new rule we were leaving some gap that was formerly covered by common law offences. Before we put this section into the bill we went carefully over the records and checked with the provincial law enforcement officers to get a full list of all the common law crimes that had been charged in Canada since the code was first passed in 1892. All of those common law crimes which have been charged in the interval have now been incorporated in the present Criminal Code bill. The only possible gap there mignt now be would be if there were some form of common law crime which we have not had occasion to charge in past Canadian history. We think if a case of that kind were to come up-and it seems most unlikely-it might be better at that time to bring in an amendment to the Criminal Code making provision for such an offence. For we believe if we are to have a Criminal Code in Canada it is desirable that we should be in a position to say to all Canadians, "Here is an exhaustive list of Canadian crimes. Unless the offence can be found in this code it cannot be charged."

On section 16-Insanity.

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: This is one of the sections which deserve consideration, and cannot be carried quickly. It covers the whole defence of insanity, and is one of the most important sections in the Criminal Code.

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: Before the minister deals with any particular point of view, would he tell us when it is anticipated that the royal commission to which this subject will be referred will be set up. Has he in mind any of the persons who will be appointed to it?

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE

Yes. As the hon. member for Prince Albert has said, this is an important section in that it sets out the defence of insanity. As the hon. member for Kamloops has indicated, it is a matter which we had proposed to remit to a royal commission for consideration. It is our wish to set up that commission at the earliest possible moment.
I may say that already I have been discussing the matter with a man whose eminence and abilities in our opinion entitle him to consideration as a possible chairman of the royal commission, and I have discussed with him the possibility of finding time from his other preoccupations to act for us in this capacity. I have received a tentatively favourable answer, but he has not been able to assure me formally that he can act until he takes up with his colleagues the matter of whether he can get the necessary time off. However, as soon as he, or smother person of equal ability, agrees, we can proceed to collect the

other personnel. We do wish to set up the commission as soon as we possibly can.

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE

It is possible; but on second

Therefore I suggested to hon. members that these subject matters which are being remitted, in the one case to the royal commission and in three others to a special parliamentary joint committee, might be passed in their present form in order that we should have that part of the law covered; and then when we get the reports back from the royal commission and the parliamentary committee we would proceed to bring in amendments to carry into effect their recommendations.

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext:
In connection with the
royal commission, can the minister take the committee into his confidence a little and say how many members are going to be on this commission, and whether it is intended to have on the commission at least as many who have been outstanding counsel for the defence as those who have been crown counsel; for this is the type of section that deserves the consideration of a commission on which neither crown nor defence shall be overweighted.
This is a section that more and more is affording a defence to those charged particularly with capital offences. The reason for that is simply the fact, as someone said the other day-and I am not referring to another debate, Mr. Chairman-that if juries can find reasonable grounds for believing that insanity exists to such an extent as to have dethroned the reason of the person charged with the offence, they bring in verdicts of manslaughter even when manslaughter ought not to be the verdict, but in point of fact the verdict should be not guilty by reason of insanity. Certainly the law of insanity as applied today does not meet with the advances that have been made in recent years in the matter of mental diseases.
This is a section that will deserve the serious attention not only of the committee of parliament and of the royal commission that is to be set up, but the utmost consideration on the part of penologists and those who are specialists in mental diseases, so as to bring the criminal law up to date. As
Criminal Code
the minister knows, this is one of the major means of exculpation that exist today in the criminal law.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE

I am in complete agreement
with my hon. friend as to the importance of this subject. We are hopeful that we can get men-and we think on this commission we should have at least one lady-of real eminence in their fields. We think, although this is not a final decision by any means, that the number of the royal commission might properly be seven. We have no idea of making it up entirely of lawyers-either for the prosecution or for the defence-because we think that there should be at least one psychiatrist upon it, in view of the fact that the subject of psychiatry is involved.
In our search for proper candidates for such a commission we not only have to find men and women who are properly equipped, but in these busy days it is sometimes very difficult to find those who are properly qualified and who also have the necessary time which they can devote to work of this sort. Sometimes a first-rate potential appointee simply cannot get the necessary leisure from his other duties in order to discharge a task of this sort. We want to have legal representation on it; we want to have the fair sex represented; we want to have psychiatrists represented. But we do not think it would be appropriate to have the commission made up of psychiatrists and lawyers. And seven is the number we have in mind.

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE

Would there be some merit in separating the words "immediate death or grievous bodily harm"? A person may believe that the person compelling him may carry out the crime of murder, let us say, at the point of a gun, and that may well be an excuse for committing this offence; whereas the threat of grievous bodily harm could very well not be accepted. subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: On section 77, Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask the minister why the new section was not left to common law rule. Before the establishment of this section was this not the rule of law under the Criminal Code, and why was it necessary to make a new section?

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, section 81 reads as follows:
(1) Every one who
(a)	engages as a principal in a prize fight,
(b)	advises, encourages or promotes a prize fight, or
(c)	is present at a prize fight as an aid, second, surgeon, umpire, backer, or reporter, is guilty o 1 an offence . . .
"Prize fight" is defined as:
... an encounter or fight with fists or hands between two persons who have met for that purpose by previous arrangement . . .
What is the difference between a prize fight and a boxing contest? I see no reason why this section should be continued at all. At the time it was actually made law it was a serious offence to hold prize fights and in 1913 or 1914, I believe it was, I remember the occasion in Calgary when Arthur Pelky was indicted for manslaughter arising out of a prize fight held with the then champion of the world, Luther McCarthy. As far as the jury were concerned they said the law was there, but they brought in an acquittal. I would ask the minister how many times this section has been used since 1914, and why it is necessary to incorporate a section in the law which to all intents and purposes has no application today.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think if my hon. friend had just kept on reading the section-

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: I know the section.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext:
-beyond the point where he left off he would have found the answer to
Criminal Code
his question. Perhaps I had better read the whole of paragraph 2 of section 81, which reads as follows:
In this section, "prize fight"-
-the participation in which is the offence specified in the first subsection of this section-
-means an encounter or fight with fists or hands between two persons who have met for that purpose by previous arrangement made by or for them, but a boxing contest between amateur sportsmen,-

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: Yes, between amateur sportsmen.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext:
Yes, but just let me finish.
-but a boxing contest between amateur sportsmen, where the contestants wear boxing gloves of not less than five ounces each in weight-
Now here it is here.
-or any boxing contest held with the permission or under the authority of an athletic board or commission or similar body established by or under the authority of the legislature of a province for the control of sport within the province, shall be deemed not to be a prize fight.
In other words, in the course of consolidating the code we have dropped the present sections 104, 107, 108, 627, and 628 because they are no longer of any use, and because most boxing contests are now staged under the authority of a provincial boxing commission. The only residual offence to which this section relates is a professional prize fight staged outside the authority and control of a provincial commission. I am sure my hon. friend would agree it is desirable, if we are going to control boxing, that we be able to prohibit all unauthorized contests.

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: I would like to ask the minister how many provinces have no athletic boards today. Are there not only three provinces with this type of board or commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I cannot answer that question, but if my hon. friend suggests three, my view would be that there were more. There must be commissions of that sort in British Columbia, Alberta, I think Saskatchewan, certainly in Manitoba and Ontario, and they have prize fights in Quebec.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: Prize fights?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: I beg your pardon; boxing contests within the meaning of the act.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: You will be in a fight if you say that.

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext:
I do not think the minister has made that section very clear, to me at any rate. It would appear a prize fight means an encounter where boxing gloves are not used,

Criminal Code
and in the latter part of the section it states that in a boxing contest gloves must be used. I do not know very much about prize fights, but I understand that in all prize fights today boxing gloves are used. I do not see the difference, since all boxing contests today are fought for a prize. There is a cash prize for one person, or it is divided between the two. Under this section could a prize fight with gloves between two professional boxers be allowed if authorized by these boxing commissions?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext:
Yes, I think so. It would mean that-
. . . any boxing contest held with the permission or under the authority of an athletic board or commission or similar body established by or under the authority of the legislature of a province for the control of sport within the province, shall be deemed not to be a prize fight.
In other words, if amateur sportsmen desire to get together at the Y.M.C.A., at an athletic club, a boys' camp or something of that sort, not for money but as amateurs and have a boxing match, and wear gloves of at least five ounces in weight, they are not covered by the section. Nor does the section cover contests which are held under the auspices of a provincial commission set up for that purpose. However, other contests are covered.
With his usual acumen my hon. friend has put his finger on the point. If money is involved, if they are not amateurs, and if they do not have the authority of the provincial commission, then they have committed an offence under the section. The purpose of the section, having regard to the point which was raised by my hon. friend the member for Prince Albert, is to cover all efforts to stage a professional prize fight which has not been authorized by a provincial boxing commission.

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext:
I have no specific amendment to suggest or anything of that nature, but I want to ask the minister whether he is able to say what consideration was given, as a matter of general policy, to making it more difficult to obtain pistols or revolvers. While I observe that section 84 continues section 117 and therefore is not any new law, it seems to me to make it easier or to lay down a certain immunity for a person who carries a pistol or revolver, whatever may be the intent with which he is carrying it. I should have thought that it might be somewhat more difficult for a person who has a

nefarious intention to carry out that intention with a shotgun than with a pistol or a revolver; yet he is prohibited from carrying a shotgun, even a sawed-off shotgun. In other words if he can conceal his shotgun he might carry out his intention with immunity.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: It is only a sawed-off shotgun that could be tucked inside one's coat.

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: That is the point exactly. The other type of weapon cannot be concealed. A pistol or a revolver is easily concealed. Therefore I am wondering why section 84 was not changed. A pistol or revolver can be concealed very easily. It seems to me that the person who carries a pistol or a revolver should be under some onus to explain for what purpose he is carrying it. He is not guilty of an offence under section 84. Perhaps, to make the matter clearer, I should put it in this way. By section 84 he is absolved from committing an offence when he carries a pistol or a revolver.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext:
No. Section 84 provides as follows:
Every one who carries concealed an offensive weapon other than a pistol or revolver is guilty of an offence punishable on summary conviction.

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: But in another part of this little code on firearms my hon. friend will see that, in order to carry a pistol or a revolver, he must get a permit from the police to do so.

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: I know that. But in order to carry a shotgun you have to have a licence.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: No; not a shotgun.

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: Not under this section, but under most provincial statutes you do.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: Oh.

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: The point I am raising is the general point as to whether it would not be desirable to make it more difficult to obtain pistols and revolvers. I know there are some authorized revolver clubs. I am not suggesting that their activities should be curtailed in any way. I am really asking what consideration was given to making it more difficult to obtain pistols and revolvers in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: As a member of the last parliament my hon. friend will recall that in the year 1951, if I remember aright, I brought into the house all these sections dealing with firearms that we now see in this new Bill 7 pretty much unchanged. At that time this code of law dealing with the possession and the registration of firearms had been passed upon by the mounted police in consultation with the various police forces in Canada. I think it was in view of this recent consideration of the whole subject matter that the royal commission and all the subsequent bodies who have considered this Bill No. 7 thought the law in this respect was quite up to date and hence left it pretty much in the form in which it was brought into the house in 1951.

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: I should like to ask a question with regard to section 84. Having regard to the reading of the section, what is the position of a man out in the woods who has a hunting knife underneath his mackinaw? Is that against the law here? I know that is the regular thing out in the woods. It might also be interesting to know what is the position of the policeman, because he has a baton underneath his coat and that is described as an offensive weapon, I know.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will look at page 4 in the interpretation section at the beginning of the bill, he will see that "offensive weapon" is defined. It will be found at the bottom of page 4, paragraph 29. The definition reads as follows:
"offensive weapon" or "weapon" means
(a)	anything that is designed to be used as a weapon and
(b)	anything that a person uses or intends to use as a weapon, whether or not it is designed to be used as a weapon, and, without restricting the generality of the foregoing, includes a firearm, air-gun or air-pistol and ammunition for a firearm, air-gun or air-pistol;
It may be the case that, under that definition, the possession of the knife would be regarded as an offensive weapon, although I wonder. Would one consider that the knife which the person my hon. friend has in mind, out in a camp and which he has in his pack for perfectly peaceful purposes, was designed to be used as a weapon? Would he say that knife was designed to be used as a weapon? I suppose that argument could be made, but I cannot conceive of any prosecution ever being launched against such an individual unless it was under some set of circumstances in which it appeared that he intended to use it as such. I do not think there is much likelihood, for example, that if a chap out hunting has a hunting knife along with him to skin a moose he has killed, the mounted police are going to come along, pick him up and charge him with
Criminal Code
carrying an offensive weapon. It depends on the circumstances of the individual case.

Section agreed to.

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext:
I am interested in knowing the reason for the need for protection of those who are at a public meeting. Section 87 reads as follows:
Notwithstanding anything in this act, every one who has an offensive weapon in his possession while he is attending or is on his way to attend a public meeting is guilty of an offence punishable on summary conviction.
This is a new section. I was wondering whether the law previously lacked any provision designed to protect those who are at public meetings, or the reason for this new section.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: Well-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext:
Does that include rotten
tomatoes?

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE

My answer to that would be
an unhesitating no. A provision to this effect was in the law prior to 1951. It was then removed, and it has been thought desirable to restore it. As to its purpose, I think it is obvious from a perusal of the section. It is to guard against people carrying offensive weapons to public meetings.

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext:
Possibly the minister
will explain what was the justification for removal in 1951 and the need for restoration in 1954. Has anything happened in the interval? Have there been any incidents at public meetings for which there was no applicable punishment for the carrying of such instruments?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext:
The note I have on this
clause is that it was felt that persons should be prohibited from attending public meetings while armed, whether or not they had permits to carry revolvers. A man having a permit to carry a revolver or pistol could, in the absence of a clause like this, rely upon his permit to carry it to a public meeting. Under section 619 justices had power to seize offensive weapons from persons attending public meetings. Sections 620 and 621 provided for the restoration of such weapons after seizure. It was felt that these weapons should not be restored but should be forfeited.
As the result of the inclusion of this section, however, sections 619, 620 and 621 have been dropped. In other words, instead of having the provision that was in the law previously, namely that a justice of the peace

Criminal Code
could go and take these weapons away from a man, it was thought that there was more common sense in saying that he could not take them there in the first place, and that if he did it would be an offence.

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: Is it to protect political speakers?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Prince
Albert raises an important point. He asks whether it is designed to protect political speakers. If that were so I would say it would be a very laudable objective.

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext:
I regret very much that this
clause is new. It should have been in force at the time my father was in politics, when Sir Charles Tupper was prime minister of Canada and the Intercolonial Railway kept men at the Riviere du Loup shops to use crowbars and other iron bars to disturb Liberal meetings. He is not ignorant at all. He did me the great honour of asking me to explain this matter. That was a great honour. With all his wisdom and experience I think he should have explained it. But as he does not require an explanation from himself, he is asking me the very question we are asking the minister who introduced this bill. Surely it is an axiom that, before passing legislation,

we should ask from the one who introduces it just what is the purpose of it, the meaning and the interpretation.
I have just one further word to say. The question of what is reasonable will have as many interpretations as there are police officers. Any clarification on that point that can be obtained will be most useful, and also with reference to the search of premises without a warrant. We must go every step of the way that is required to give police officers the means to protect property and society, but I would emphasize again that in the granting of such authority we must also not overstep the mark so far as the protection of the civil rights of the people of Canada is concerned.

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: I thank my hon. friend for his little speech. I am sorry there was no more enlightenment, but I will explain to him what I understand by this provision of the law. I wonder what his reaction will be and whether or not he will agree with me. We must take a classic case. Police constables are on duty on a street and they hear the noise of guns. They go to the corner, and they see a man running away. They cannot recognize him because they see him from the back, and looking at him from a distance they see him go into a house. They have not seen his face. They go into the house and they see some men there wearing clothes of the same colour as those of the man they are pursuing. Would my hon. friend have any objection to the searching of those men by the constables who were running after a man who went into the house?

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: No.

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: Well, then, that is a reasonable ground.

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: May I point out to the hon. member that he has not read the clause. Dwelling houses are exempt. Policemen cannot enter dwelling houses without a warrant.

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext:
Then the law should be amended in order to include rooming houses. I want my hon. friends, or any one of them, to mention the flaw in the law. The law must be more severe than it is now to meet emergencies, and of course most arrests are emergency arrests. I could ask the Minister of Justice whether the largest number of arrests are not made without warrants right on the spot by the constabulary, whether federal, provincial or municipal. These men are on duty to protect human life and property, and when they receive a telephone call at night they do not go to a magistrate to get a warrant. They are on the spot and they make the arrest. This is how they do

it, and I am not speaking as a lawyer. I am speaking as a man on the street. It is general knowledge. Therefore they must be empowered to act.
I will agree with the hon. member for Vancouver East that there are some constables who have no judgment. It happens in any class of society. There are men without judgment, and there may be errors. It is unfortunate, but on the other hand there must be protection of the people. This is very important, and this is the very reason we are now discussing this piece of legislation. It is all right, as my hon. friend has said, to protect liberty and freedom, but those who want to enjoy liberty and freedom must abide by the law of the land. I do not see why we should be more indulgent to thugs, bandits, housebreakers and all those who create disorder and are a plague on society.
The other day I heard one hon. member say that in the future when we are more civilized punishment will not be so harsh as it is now, and that this will be a sign of progress. What I maintain is that progress will be achieved through abiding by the law. That will be progress. When constables are on duty and risking their lives to protect the Canadian people they deserve consideration. They are not all perfect. I give some of them the benefit of the doubt. They are entitled to it because they risk their lives at every moment of the day.
My hon. friend enjoys liberty. I do also, and we all do, but we want the Canadian people to enjoy the same liberty that those who do not respect the law are supposed to have, according to some hon. members. If I spoke in a jocular or light vein in the first place, I am very serious now. There are those who contend, like the hon. gentleman, that we will have progress in Canada when the law is not respected or when those who infringe the law go scot free, but I say if that happens we will have chaos and anarchy in the country. I want order in the country. I want good government, and we have it. I want order, and I hope we will have it. That is the purpose of the Criminal Code of Canada.
Sir, there were ten commandments given by Jehovah to Moses a long time ago by which the world was ruled for centuries, and the penalty was to come from God in the other world. But now mankind has grown so wicked that there cannot be enough law to maintain order not only in this country but in all countries of the world. Therefore I hope that my hon. friend will realize that
Criminal Code
it is important to have an enactment like this which will permit constables to protect human life and property in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext:
As I was saying, Mr. Chairman, I doubt very much whether I can improve upon the excellent explanation which was given by the member for Vancouver-Kingsway. Let me take the case which was cited by the hon. member for Vancouver East, and I discuss this with some modesty. If a police officer proposed to search me without a warrant, merely because he saw me waiting for my wife, he would not be acting upon reasonable grounds, I suggest, under all the circumstances.
On the other hand, if a police officer were looking around at night in a dark alleyway at the back of a warehouse and discovered one man lifting another through a window which had just been broken open, and he proceeded to search them for weapons, I would think he would be acting upon reasonable grounds. As to whether, between those two extremes, the facts of a particular case constitute reasonable grounds, that is a matter the peace officer must establish in each case in order to justify his search. The idea that he can just do these things without reasonable grounds and shrug off responsibility is without foundation.
If the hon. member for Vancouver East will go back to section 28 and following sections in this bill he will see there set out the circumstances under which a peace officer is protected from criminal or civil liability in respect of the actions which he takes as a peace officer. In a free, democratic country, such as we have in Canada, a peace officer has little more power than the average citizen. He is strictly answerable for his conduct. He must find, under the code, legal support for whatever action he takes.
Now, it may be that in so far as his civil liability is concerned he would not have the financial resources to make a suit for damages worth while. But I am sure the hon. member

has heard of cases in which a private detective operating in and for a department store detained a person suspected of shoplifting upon what he thought were reasonable grounds, and to his consternation discovered later that his employer was on the receiving end of a heavy suit for damages. That is the kind of liability which arises when a peace 'officer exceeds his powers under the law.
In this particular case, as has been explained by other speakers, the question with which we are faced is whether we shall ask a peace officer, when he finds men under those conditions I have cited-in the course of breaking into a warehouse-to get a police magistrate or justice of the peace out of bed in the middle of the night to obtain a warrant and then go back to search or arrest the men. The only other way in which he could make a search is upon reasonable grounds.
I must confess that when I first saw the section my reaction was somewhat along the lines of that of the hon. member for Vancouver East. When I read that a peace officer had the power to search a structure, I rather objected until I saw that a dwelling was excepted from it, and that as a result our homes were still our castles. When this section is confined to those cases in which reasonable grounds can be shown, and when it only applies to premises that are not dwellings, I really do not think it is as exceptional as the hon. member for Vancouver East has thought.

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: To my mind the minister's explanation leaves one point obscure which I think the house ought to appreciate. The object of this section is to give the peace officer power to search vehicles and premises only in a limited number of cases. In the cases that have been presented to the house we have had conjured up crimes of violence, forcible entry and robbery. Those cases are not covered by this section. The code does contain, and very properly, provisions which not only permit but exhort even ordinary citizens to arrest persons committing acts of violence. It is the duty of people to do that, without any such section as we have here. This section gives the peace officer the right in a limited number of cases, namely cases involving carrying firearms-am I right?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext:
No. According to section 82-
Every one who carries or has in his custody or possession an offensive weapon for a purpose dangerous to the public peace-
In other words, if a burglar is going through a window he can be searched to see if he has a revolver on him.

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: I follow what the minister says, but the section is limited to searches under sections 82 to 91, and those sections involve carrying or dealing in offensive weapons or firearms. For example, section 84, which we discussed earlier, deals with concealed weapons. A peace officer may come up to a person on the street, and noting a bulge in his coat conclude that he had a concealed weapon. Then, if his grounds were reasonable, he could make a search to make sure whether it was or was not a concealed weapon. But that is not the kind of offence where anyone is immediately in danger. So I do think the committee should appreciate that this sort of leeway given to a police officer is for a different kind of case from the hot pursuit of a criminal who has just committed a crime, or when a crime of violence is imminent.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: With great respect to the hon. member I suggest that he might keep in mind the very case I cited, that dealing with the two men who got through a warehouse window in the middle of the night. minister has said, but I do not believe I follow his reasoning exactly. The person to whom the minister has referred, who enters a warehouse for the purpose of committing a robbery, would be committing the crime of breaking and entering.

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE

speechtext: Under this section would a police officer be privileged to, let us say, pick up a youth if he thought the youth had in his possession certain things taken from a building that had been entered? Could he pick up that youth, if he saw him in that area?

person on some fancied or unreasonable grounds because he thought such person was guilty of a crime, and used this section as an excuse, it would not protect him from proceedings for unlawful arrest?

(2)	Every one commits an offence who, being a party to a contract with the government directly or indirectly subscribes, gives, or agrees to subscribe or give, to any person any valuable consideration
(a)	for the purpose of promoting the election of a candidate or a class or party of candidates to the parliament of Canada or the legislature, or
(b)	with intent to influence or affect in any way the result of an election conducted for the purpose of electing persons to serve in the parliament of Canada or the legislature.
(3)	Every one who commits an offence under this section is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for five years.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre asked a pertinent question, as to whether the government has been serious about this section and if there have been prosecutions. I was on the point of asking if anything had been done about the questioning by Mr. Skey. He asked Mr. Hilton whether Mr. Hilton had come to Ottawa to make representations to the wartime prices and trade board with a view to increasing their income by $2,500,000, and Mr. Hilton had. I submit, Mr. Chairman-

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, surely the purpose of this committee is to study these sections and see whether they are desirable or whether they should be amended. If the wording is agreeable they should be passed. We are not here to examine some specific act that may or may not have occurred or to examine some alleged offence against the section. We are here simply to determine whether a section is good or bad law and whether it should be adopted, and if it is not good law how it should be changed. We are not here to try any alleged offence but simply to look at the wording and to see if it is desirable law for the people of Canada.

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: I am not taking any risks whatsoever when I read from a record placed before the house some years ago. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I can certainly disabuse my hon. friend's mind so far as I am concerned, because I was not here in 1946.
